summaries.example: Mia says, “I think the red box has a toy.” Later, she learns that the red box is also called “the box by the window.” Her two sentences may point to the same box, but they can feel different to Mia because she knows the box in two different ways. Philosophers ask how to describe what Mia believes without saying she is simply confused.
summaries.summary: A propositional attitude report tells us about someone’s mental connection to what a sentence says. For example, “Jill believes that Jack broke his crown” reports a belief. The central puzzle comes from cases where two names point to the same person, yet a person may accept one sentence and reject another. Lois Lane may believe that Superman is strong while not believing that Clark Kent is strong, even though Superman and Clark Kent are the same person. Philosophers disagree about how to explain this. Frege says that names have both a reference and a sense, or way of presenting their reference. Some Russell-inspired theories say the belief concerns the person and property themselves, while the difference may come from how the belief is held or from what a speaker suggests. Other theories make the explanation depend on context, or question whether beliefs are structured propositions at all. The entry also examines further puzzles involving translation, names used in different ways, and reports made by someone who is confused about identities.
key_ideas: Words can point to the same thing but still matter in different ways when we describe someone’s beliefs.
Frege’s puzzle asks why replacing one name with another name for the same object can change a belief report.
Some philosophers focus on a person’s way of thinking; others focus on the object and property involved.
The entry compares several theories and also discusses puzzles about context, names, and language.
summaries.why_it_matters: We use belief and knowledge reports constantly when we explain people’s choices, plans, mistakes, and reasons. A good theory should explain why a person can seem reasonable while thinking about one person in two different ways. It should also explain how language communicates more than simple true-or-false information. These questions connect the study of language with the study of thought and knowledge.

important_terms.definition: A sentence about someone’s believing, hoping, knowing, or having another mental attitude toward what a sentence says.
What a sentence says or means, such as the claim that a box has a toy.
The thing or person that a name or phrase points to.
The way someone thinks about or recognizes something, even when two names point to the same thing.

questions_to_think_about: Can you believe two sentences that describe the same thing but think about it differently?
If two names point to the same person, should they always be interchangeable in a sentence about belief?
How might the words someone uses help us understand what they believe?
Could a belief report be true but still give a listener the wrong impression?

summaries.example: Suppose Ava has met a musician called “Alex” and has also read about a politician called “Alex.” She does not realize they are the same individual. She may sincerely accept “Alex is a musician” when thinking of the musician and reject “Alex is a musician” when thinking of the politician. Kripke-style cases use this kind of identity confusion to show that a theory must explain not only the names in a report, but also how context and the believer’s cognitive perspective affect what the report communicates.
summaries.summary: Propositional attitude reports describe cognitive relations to propositions, as in “Lois believes that Superman is strong.” They generate a major problem for theories of meaning because co-referring names appear not to be freely substitutable inside attitude reports. Lois can believe that Superman is strong while denying that Clark Kent is strong, although the names refer to the same individual. The same issue appears in ordinary sentences: “Superman is strong” and “Clark Kent is strong” have the same truth-value, yet they can differ in cognitive significance for Lois. Frege’s solution distinguishes reference from sense. In an attitude context, he holds that an expression is relevant through a mode of presentation, allowing the reports to differ. Critics object that this can conflict with ordinary reference, anaphora, indexicals, common reports about many people, and apparently valid entailments. Neo-Russellian theories instead treat some thoughts as singular propositions containing objects directly. Naive Russellians accept that the two reports have the same fundamental truth-conditions and explain the apparent difference through pragmatic implicature or a distinction between belief content and belief state. Other neo-Russellians use contextualist strategies so that the way a proposition is grasped affects the report without changing the proposition itself. The entry also examines sententialism, paratactic accounts, interpreted logical forms, and unstructured propositions. Each approach must explain both apparent substitution failures and ordinary entailments. Kripke’s puzzles involving translation and repeated names, and Richard’s puzzle involving an ascriber’s identity ignorance, show that the issue concerns the practice of reporting attitudes, not merely the meaning
key_ideas: Frege’s puzzle combines two observations: co-referring names can differ in cognitive significance, and corresponding belief reports can differ in apparent truth-value.
Frege explains the difference by distinguishing sense from reference and by making attitude contexts sensitive to sense.
Naive Russellian theories treat the relevant belief content as a singular proposition and explain some differences through pragmatic information about how the belief is held.
Contextualist theories try to preserve direct reference while allowing the context or an implicit way of grasping a proposition to affect truth.
The entry also considers sentential and other non-structured theories, but these face problems with translation, entailment, implicit beliefs, or the fine-grained character of thought.
Kripke’s and Richard’s puzzles show that a complete theory must handle translation, repeated names, indexicals, and identity mistakes by the reporter as well as by the believer.
summaries.why_it_matters: Belief reports sit at the intersection of semantics, philosophy of mind, epistemology, metaphysics, and theories of communication. They help explain why people can act rationally while accepting apparently conflicting descriptions, and why a report can be literally accurate yet misleading about how someone thinks. The debate also tests broader principles about reference, translation, context, and the relationship between what language says and what speakers convey. An adequate theory must account for truth, rationality, prediction, explanation, and communication together.

important_terms.definition: A sentence that attributes believing, hoping, knowing, desiring, or another mental relation to what a clause expresses.
Frege’s term for the way an expression presents its referent; co-referring expressions can have different senses.
The object, person, or entity to which an expression refers.
The principle that replacing one expression with another having the same reference should preserve truth; attitude contexts create an apparent challenge to it.
A theory holding that some thoughts have an object itself as a direct constituent, rather than representing it through a descriptive surrogate.
The view that the content or truth of an attitude report can vary with features of the conversational setting.
The claim that thought-objects are structured, abstract propositions whose parts correspond in some way to linguistic structure.
Information suggested by an utterance beyond what its literal semantic content encodes.

questions_to_think_about: Should a belief report state only what someone believes, or also how that person thinks of what they believe?
Can pragmatic communication explain why one report sounds misleading without making it false?
What should count as believing the same proposition when two people use different concepts or words?
Why might indexicals such as “I,” “you,” and “he” be difficult for a simple Fregean theory?
Does a theory of belief need structured propositions, or could sets of possible worlds do the work?

summaries.example: Jordan knows two students, Sam and Taylor. Jordan does not know that Sam is Taylor. Jordan may say, “Sam won the contest,” but deny, “Taylor won the contest,” even though both names refer to the same student. A friend reporting Jordan’s thoughts has to decide whether to describe only the student and the contest result, or also the different ways Jordan identifies that student. That is the kind of problem philosophers study in attitude reports.
summaries.summary: Propositional attitude reports tell us about mental attitudes such as belief, hope, and knowledge. They often use a verb followed by a clause, as in “Jordan believes that the team won,” though other forms are possible. The central issue is Frege’s puzzle. Two names can refer to the same person, yet someone can accept a sentence containing one name and reject a sentence containing the other. Lois Lane’s beliefs about Superman and Clark Kent make this vivid: she can believe that Superman is strong without believing that Clark Kent is strong. Frege’s theory says that a name has a reference and a sense. The sense is a way of presenting the reference, and attitude reports are sensitive to this difference. Critics worry about pronouns, demonstrations, reports about groups, and cases where the reporter’s wording does not match the believer’s perspective. Russell-inspired theories emphasize direct relations to objects and distinguish what is believed from the way it is believed. A simple version says that apparently different reports may have the same truth conditions but different pragmatic effects. Contextualist theories instead allow the setting or an implicit way of grasping a proposition to affect the report. The entry also considers views that treat attitudes as relations to sentences or other linguistic structures, and views that reject structured propositions. Finally, Kripke’s and Richard’s puzzles show that translation, repeated names, and the reporter’s own mistaken identities must be included in any full account.
key_ideas: The main puzzle is that two names for the same person may behave differently in a report about what someone believes.
Frege explains this with a difference between reference and sense, or a way of thinking about the reference.
Russell-inspired philosophers argue that some thoughts are directly about objects, but they still need to explain identity mistakes.
Some theories say the report is literally about the same proposition but suggests different information about how the person believes it.
Other theories make context part of the truth conditions of the report.
The entry compares these views and points out problems involving pronouns, translation, repeated names, and beliefs about beliefs.
summaries.why_it_matters: We rely on attitude reports to explain why people act, what they know, and why they make mistakes. The topic shows that communication is not only a matter of naming objects and checking truth-values. The same words can guide different expectations about a person’s behavior, depending on how that person thinks. Studying these reports helps philosophers investigate the boundary between literal meaning, thought, and conversational suggestion.

important_terms.definition: A sentence that reports someone’s believing, knowing, hoping, or another mental attitude toward what a sentence expresses.
The object or person a word or name stands for.
The way an expression presents its reference to a thinker; two names can have different senses while sharing a reference.
The idea that a name may contribute the object it refers to directly to a thought or proposition.
The extra message a speaker commonly gives through an utterance, beyond its basic literal meaning.
A theory saying that the meaning or truth of an attitude report depends partly on the surrounding conversational situation.

questions_to_think_about: If Sam and Taylor are the same person, why might Jordan accept one sentence and reject the other?
Is a report misleading necessarily false?
Should a theory describe what someone believes, how they believe it, or both?
Why do words such as “I,” “you,” and “he” create special problems in reports?
What can happen when the person making a report is the one who is confused?
